analysis.one_liner: Created an independent board to police company audits and made executives personally answerable for false financial reports.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 97-0 in July 2002 and it went on to become the Sarbanes-Oxley law, the biggest overhaul of corporate auditing and executive accountability since the 1930s.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron and WorldCom collapses wiped out retirement savings, this bill created a new oversight board to regulate the accounting firms that audit public companies, banned auditors from doing consulting work for the same clients they audit, required CEOs and CFOs to personally certify their companies' financial statements, and added criminal penalties for corporate fraud and document destruction. It also banned companies from making personal loans to executives, forced faster disclosure of executive stock sales, and protected employees who report fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who owns stock or has a retirement account invested in public companies: the bill aimed to make the numbers they rely on honest. Employees gained protection against being fired for reporting fraud and a ban on executives dumping their own stock during pension blackout periods, when workers are locked out of trading.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors, retirement savers, and company employees

how_it_helps.text: Establishes the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board to register audit firms, set standards, inspect them, and impose sanctions, replacing industry self-policing [S3].

Requires CEOs and CFOs to certify that financial statements fairly present the company's condition, and requires them to forfeit bonuses and profits after an accounting restatement caused by misconduct [S3].

Bars auditors from performing listed non-audit services like bookkeeping and valuation for the same clients they audit, and mandates five-year audit partner rotation, to keep auditors independent of the companies they are policing [S3].
Prohibits insider trades by executives during pension fund blackout periods, when ordinary employees cannot trade, with profits recoverable by the company [S3].
Adds criminal penalties for destroying records to obstruct investigations and for defrauding shareholders of public companies, and raises penalties for securities fraud and obstruction [S4].
Prohibits publicly traded companies from punishing employees who assist fraud investigations, with remedies including reinstatement, back pay, and damages [S4].
Prohibits corporations from making personal loans to their executives, closing a loophole used by companies like WorldCom [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Public companies and their shareholders bear the cost: audit firms must register and pay fees, executives face certification and clawback rules, and companies fund the new oversight board through mandatory fees. Compliance costs for internal-control reporting fall on companies and are passed to shareholders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public companies, their executives, and auditors

drawbacks.text: The oversight board and the accounting standard setter are funded by mandatory fees assessed on public companies, allocated by market capitalization, which raises costs for companies and ultimately their shareholders [S5].

Liability against accounting firms is restricted to intentional conduct or repeated negligent conduct, a limit the industry sought; critics of the law have also pointed to the compliance burden of internal-control reporting, which falls hardest on smaller public companies [S3].

The bill bans a list of non-audit services but leaves other consulting services allowed with audit-committee preapproval, and a Senate-passed provision on corporate tax returns was only a nonbinding statement of the Senate's view, not an enforceable rule [S4, S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and durable: honest audits protect the savings of every shareholder and retirement saver, and the criminal and clawback provisions changed executive behavior. The honest cost is real but narrower: audit and compliance fees went up, small public companies bore disproportionate paperwork costs, and the accounting industry kept its government-backed position as the mandatory channel for audits.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 97-0, folded it into a parallel House bill, and the combined version was signed into law as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act at the end of July 2002.

narrative.text: The Senate Banking Committee reported the bill as an original measure on June 18, 2002, and the Senate took it up within weeks, amid public anger over the Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals [S7].

The Senate invoked cloture on the bill by a 91-2 vote on July 12, 2002, with 46 of 50 Democrats and 44 of 49 Republicans voting yes; a motion by Senator McCain to recommit the bill to committee failed and a second recommittal motion was ruled out of order [S7, S8].
The Senate passed the bill 97-0 on July 15, 2002, with every senator voting in favor, including all 50 Democrats, 46 of 49 Republicans, and the independent [S7, S9].

The Senate then incorporated the measure into the parallel House bill, H.R. 3763, as an amendment, vitiated its separate passage, and the combined bill was enacted later in July 2002 as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary investors, retirement savers, and employees gained audit oversight, executive accountability, and fraud penalties they did not have before. The largest audit firms and corporate executives accepted tighter rules but the accounting industry's role as auditors of every public company was locked in.

sides.party_line_note: There was essentially no partisan fight: cloture passed 91-2 with 46 of 50 Democrats and 44 of 49 Republicans in favor, and final passage was 97-0 with every Democrat, Republican, and independent voting yes.

industries.note: The bill strips them of lucrative non-audit consulting revenue for audit clients, mandates partner rotation, and subjects them to board registration, inspections, and sanctions. At the same time, it locks in their position: every public company must hire a registered audit firm, and the bill directed a study of industry consolidation rather than restructuring it.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and directors of public companies
industries.note: CEOs and CFOs must personally certify financial statements, forfeit bonuses after restatements caused by misconduct, face criminal penalties for certifying false reports, and can no longer receive personal loans from their companies. Their interest in keeping lax rules ran against the public's interest in honest financial reporting.

Companies face higher audit and compliance costs, including mandatory fees to fund the oversight board, and stricter disclosure of off-balance-sheet deals and executive loans. The offset is that credible audits lower the cost of raising capital from the public.

The SEC must adopt rules separating analysts from investment banking pressure and banning retaliation for unfavorable research, curbing the practice of banks' analysts promoting stocks their banks were underwriting.
